title: Move Zeroes
description: Brute force to optimized: a separate result array versus in place two pointer swapping.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of integers nums, move all zeros to the end of the array while keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements the same. This must be done in place, without making a copy of the array.

blocks.text: Given an array of integers nums, move all zeros to the end of the array while keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements the same. This must be done in place, without making a copy of the array.

blocks.title: Analogy: Sorting a Line by Sending Absentees to the Back
blocks.text: Picture a line of people where some are marked absent (the zeros). Walking down the line and pulling every present person forward, in the order they were already standing, naturally pushes every absent marker to the back without needing a second line to work from.

blocks.caption: Non-zero values keep their order, zeros end up pushed to the back

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Non-zero values in original order","1, 3, 12"],["Zeros pushed to the end","0, 0"],["Answer","[1, 3, 12, 0, 0]"]]}
{"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Non-zero values in original order","1"],["Zeros pushed to the end","0, 0"],["Answer","[1, 0, 0]"]]}

blocks.text: When every element is already zero, there are no non-zero values to move forward, so the array stays [0, 0, 0], unchanged.
Unlike Two Sum and Contains Duplicate, this problem carries an explicit in place requirement, which is worth treating as a direct hint about which family of technique actually applies here.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An explicit in place requirement, just like Reverse a String earlier in this sheet, is a strong signal toward a two pointer approach, rather than a hash based one, since no extra structure is allowed to hold anything.

Observation 2: A brute force that builds a separate result array gets every value right, but violates the actual constraint being tested, this is a case where the values are correct but the requirement itself is not met.

Observation 3: Testing nums equal to [0, 1, 0, 3, 12], every non-zero value, in the order it is encountered, needs to land at the front of the array, at a position that only advances once a non-zero value has actually been placed there.

Observation 4: Swapping the current element into that advancing insert position, rather than simply overwriting it, is what correctly leaves whatever was at the insert position, always a zero by that point, behind at the position it was swapped from, naturally pushing every zero toward the back with no extra step needed to move them there directly.
That reframing, from "collect non-zero values elsewhere" to "swap non-zero values forward in place", is what turns a values-correct-but-constraint-violating brute force into the intended solution.
Build a brand new array by first copying every non-zero value across in its original order, then filling the remaining slots with zeros, and finally copying that new array back over the original.

items: Create an empty result array of the same length.
Walk through nums, appending every non-zero value to the result array in order.
Fill the remaining slots of the result array with zeros.
Copy the result array back into nums.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Non-zero values are collected into a separate list first, since their exact count is not known in advance and the result array is easiest to build incrementally.
The number of zeros needed is derived by subtracting the count of non-zero values from the total length, rather than counting zeros in a separate pass.
A final explicit copy step writes the fully assembled result back into nums, since the problem requires nums itself, not a new array, to end up correct.

blocks.text: This preserves the relative order of the non-zero values and places every zero at the end, so it is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), for the two passes (build the result, then copy it back).
Space: O(n), for the separate result array.
Limitation: the problem explicitly asks for this to be done in place, and building an entirely separate array defeats that requirement even though the final values end up correct.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the separate array works but is disqualified: it produces the exact right values, but the problem specifically forbids using extra space proportional to the input, which this approach directly violates.

What actually needs to happen instead: every non-zero value needs to move directly within nums itself to its correct final position, with nothing copied anywhere else.

Can two pointers track this directly: yes, one pointer scans every element, and a second pointer marks the next position a non-zero value should occupy, advancing only when one is actually placed there.

Why swap instead of simply overwrite: overwriting would destroy whatever value already sat at the insert position, while swapping correctly relocates it, and since everything at or before the insert position other than the just-placed value is guaranteed to be zero, that swap is always safe.

The core idea: scan the array once, and every time a non-zero value is found, swap it into the advancing insert position.

Rearrange the array directly instead of copying it. Keep an insert position pointer starting at the front, and walk through the array with a second pointer. Every time a non-zero value is found, swap it into the insert position and advance the insert position. Because every non-zero value gets pulled forward in order, the zeros are naturally left behind and end up pushed toward the back, with no separate array needed.
Use two pointers: one walking through the whole array, and one tracking where the next non-zero value should be placed.

blocks.caption: Optimized: swap every non-zero value into the insert position as it is found

blocks.text: This works because everything at or before the insert position, aside from the value about to be swapped in, is guaranteed to already be zero, since the insert position only ever advances when a real value has just been placed there; swapping, rather than overwriting, means whatever sat at the insert position before, always a zero, is relocated to where the non-zero value used to be, rather than simply lost, so the total count of zeros and non-zero values is preserved throughout the entire scan.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The current element is zero","Nothing is swapped, the scan simply continues","The zero stays exactly where it is for now, to be pushed back later as other values pass it"],["The current element is non-zero","It is swapped into the insert position, which then advances by one","The non-zero value moves to its correct, order-preserving position, and a zero takes its old place"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant work per element.
Space: O(1), everything is rearranged directly inside the original array.
10. Further Optimization: Skipping the No Op Swap

Until the very first zero is encountered, the insert position and the scan position are exactly the same index, so every swap before that point trades an element with itself, a wasted operation. Checking whether the two positions actually differ before swapping skips these no op swaps entirely.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Scan index","Value","Insert position","Same position","Action"],"rows":[["0","1","0","yes","skip the swap, just advance"],["1","2","1","yes","skip the swap, just advance"],["2","0","2","not applicable","zero, skip entirely"],["3","3","2","no","swap needed, positions differ"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: only swap once the insert position has actually fallen behind

items: The scan and insert position indices stay identical for as long as every element examined so far has been non-zero, since the insert position advances in lockstep with the scan in that case.
A simple equality check between the two positions detects exactly this situation, and skips a swap that would only trade a value with itself.
Once the first zero has been passed, the insert position permanently falls behind the scan position, and every subsequent non-zero value genuinely needs a real swap to move forward.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the same asymptotic bound, now with fewer wasted swaps in practice.
Space: O(1), unchanged.

blocks.text: This is the standard in place partitioning pattern: an insert position pointer tracks where the next qualifying element belongs, while a second pointer scans the whole array, which reappears in many "rearrange this array in place" style problems.

items: Overwriting values with a plain assignment instead of a swap, which loses whatever non-zero value used to sit at the insert position.
Forgetting that the relative order of non-zero elements must be preserved, not just that zeros end up last.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["An array of all zeros","Should remain completely unchanged."],["An array with no zeros at all","The insert position and scan position stay equal throughout, so no real swaps happen."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly name the pattern as "in place partitioning around a condition", since the exact same two pointer shape solves other problems like partitioning even and odd numbers or partitioning around a pivot.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this in place", think: an insert position pointer and a scan pointer, swapping qualifying elements forward.
If the interviewer says "why swap instead of overwrite", think: overwriting would destroy the value already at the insert position, swapping relocates it instead.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce wasted work", think: skip the swap entirely whenever the insert position and scan position are still the same index.

Can you solve this using a single pointer and no swapping at all, by tracking only where to write zeros afterward?
How would this approach change if you needed to move zeros to the front instead of the end?

Any "rearrange this array in place around a condition" problem, where a slow scanning pointer and a faster insert position pointer is almost always the right shape.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space. Further optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space, with fewer wasted no-op swaps.

items: Pattern: in place partitioning with two pointers, one scanning the whole array, the other tracking where the next qualifying element belongs.
Core Idea: scan the array once, swapping every non-zero value into an advancing insert position, so zeros are naturally left behind and pushed toward the back with no extra array needed.
Time: O(n) for all three versions.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(1) for both the optimized and further optimized versions.
Most Important Observation: an explicit in place requirement is a strong signal toward two pointer partitioning, the same lesson already seen with Reverse a String.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce correct values with a separate array; recognizing that swapping, not overwriting, is what satisfies the in place requirement is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: scan with one pointer, swap non-zero values into an advancing insert position, zeros get left behind automatically.
